opus-5.5.text:
I think that confusion is actually very natural, and almost everyone goes through it. When you first enter research, you're coming from an environment where problems are given to you. In classes, someone has already defined the question, and there's a known answer. You just need to find it. Research flips that around. Often the hardest part is not solving the problem but figuring out which problem is worth solving in the first place.

When I started, I also felt quite lost. You read a lot of papers and everything seems to have been done already, or it feels like the people writing them are on a completely different level. You don't know whether your idea is good, whether it's trivial, or whether it's even a real problem. That uncertainty can be uncomfortable, especially for students who have always been good at getting the "right answer."

What helped me was realizing that research is a process you learn by doing, not by thinking about it in the abstract. You pick something concrete, maybe even something small, and you try to build it, make it work, and understand why it does or doesn't work. Through that process you develop taste. You start to see where the real pain points are and what people actually need. A lot of my own work came from being a user first. I was trying to get machine learning to work in practice and kept running into problems with the tools, and that frustration turned into the questions I worked on.

So I'd say the confusion isn't a sign that you're doing something wrong. It's part of the transition from being a consumer of knowledge to being someone who creates it. The key is not to wait until the confusion goes away before you start. Get your hands dirty, talk to people, and keep iterating. Over time the fog clears a bit, though honestly it never goes away completely, and maybe that's what keeps research interesting.

r001.rationale: The response says that the fog clears over time but “never goes away completely,” communicating that uncertainty can persist as one continues in research.

r002.rationale: It explains that research differs from classes because the question and answer are not already known; researchers must discover which problem is worth solving.

fable-5.1.text:
I think that confusion is actually very natural, and honestly I felt it too. When I first started, I thought research was about finding a problem nobody had solved and then solving it. But in practice you walk into a field and there are thousands of papers, everyone seems to know what they are doing, and you have no idea which direction is worth your time. That feeling of being lost is really just the gap between reading about research and actually doing it.

What I'd say to someone in that position is that the confusion usually comes from trying to pick the "right" problem from the top down. You read a lot, you try to map out the whole landscape, and the more you read the more paralyzed you get, because every direction looks either already taken or too hard. For me the thing that helped was going bottom up. Build something. Pick a concrete system or a concrete experiment, even a small one, and actually make it work end to end. When you do that, the real problems show up on their own. You hit something that's slow, or awkward, or doesn't scale, and suddenly you have a question that is yours, not one you borrowed from a survey paper.

A lot of my own work came out of that pattern. XGBoost started because I needed a gradient boosting implementation that was faster for a competition, not because I set out to write a famous library. TVM came from running into the same pain over and over trying to get models to run efficiently on different hardware. The problem found me because I was building things.

The other thing I'd tell people is that the confusion doesn't fully go away, it just changes shape. Senior researchers are also uncertain about what matters. The difference is they've learned to be comfortable making a bet, working on it for a while, and adjusting. So I'd encourage newcomers to not wait until the fog clears. Pick something you're genuinely curious about, build it, talk to people about what you found, and let the next step reveal itself. Taste in research is something you develop by doing, not something you need to have before you start.

r001.rationale: The response says confusion “doesn't fully go away” and that senior researchers remain uncertain about what matters, even after learning to make bets and work on them for a while.

r002.rationale: It links confusion to choosing a direction amid many papers and uncertainty about what is worth pursuing, but does not explain it as arising from research’s exploration of the unknown.

astra-6.text:
I think that confusion is very natural. When you first enter a field, you mostly see the finished results: papers where the problem is clearly stated, the method makes sense, and the experiments support the conclusion. But you don’t see all the uncertainty that came before that. So it’s easy to feel that everybody else knows what they’re doing and you’re the only one who doesn’t.

One useful way to start is to make the question smaller. Can you reproduce a result? Can you understand why a particular design choice matters? If you change one assumption, what happens? Those steps help you develop your own understanding, and gradually you start noticing questions that aren’t answered in the paper.

You don’t necessarily need a grand research agenda on day one. You need something concrete to explore, people to discuss it with, and a willingness to revise your thinking. Learning how to work through that confusion is itself part of learning how to do research.

r001.rationale: It describes confusion when first entering a field but does not say that it can persist after working in a research direction for a long time.

r002.rationale: It mentions uncertainty before finished results and unanswered questions, but does not explain that confusion arises because research explores the unknown.

sol-6.1.text:
I think that confusion is very natural. When you first enter a field, you usually encounter research through papers, and a paper presents a fairly clean story: here is the problem, here is the method, and here is the result. But it doesn’t show all the uncertainty that went into finding the problem in the first place. So it’s easy to think everyone else knows exactly what they’re doing and you’re the only one who doesn’t.

One useful way to start is to make that uncertainty more concrete. Pick a paper, try to understand why the authors made certain choices, and reproduce a small part of it. When something doesn’t work as you expected, or you wonder whether a particular assumption is necessary, you have something specific to investigate.

You don’t need to have a big research vision on day one. You build judgment by trying things, getting feedback, and gradually learning which questions are worth pursuing. Being confused is part of that process; the important thing is to turn the confusion into questions you can actually work on.

r001.rationale: The response describes confusion when first entering a field but does not say it can persist after someone has worked in a research direction for a long time.

r002.rationale: It connects confusion to uncertainty in finding a research problem and investigating assumptions, conveying that research involves exploring questions whose answers are not already known.
